descriptor: A heavily built Ice Age ambush cat with 18-centimetre canines. It was not a tiger, and has no close living relatives.

specimen.promptDetail: the sabre-toothed cat Smilodon seen in side profile with its mouth closed: two enormous curved blade-like upper canine teeth, each as long as the animal's whole lower jaw, hanging far down past the chin and clearly visible against the white background; a very muscular bear-like build with massive forelimbs, shoulders higher than the hips, a thick neck and a very short bobbed tail like a lynx; short tawny fur with faint spots

physical.fact: Its canines were up to 18 cm long, but its bite was only about a third as strong as a lion's. It pinned prey with its forelimbs first, then drove the teeth in with its neck muscles.

source.label: Christiansen and Harris 2005, Journal of Morphology

range.summary: Smilodon fatalis lived across North America and down the Pacific side of South America as far as Peru. The La Brea Tar Pits in Los Angeles alone have produced bones from more than 2,000 individuals, drawn to animals stuck in the asphalt and trapped in turn.

fossil.story: Smilodon ambushed bison, camels and young mammoths, built for wrestling rather than chasing. Many La Brea bones show healed injuries, which some researchers read as a sign that hurt animals were fed by a group.

threats.title: Its prey vanished
threats.detail: Most of the big plant-eaters of the Americas died out between about 13,000 and 10,000 years ago. A cat built to kill large animals had little else to fall back on.

threats.title: Heat, drought and fire
threats.detail: At La Brea the large mammals disappear about 13,000 years ago, during a spell of warming and drying when wildfires surged across southern California.

threats.title: People arrived
threats.detail: Human numbers were rising at the same time. People probably added to the pressure, by hunting the same prey and by lighting fires.

places.name: La Brea Tar Pits, Los Angeles
places.note: The richest Smilodon site on Earth, still being excavated in the middle of the city. It is California's state fossil.

places.name: Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County
places.note: Mounted skeletons from La Brea in the Age of Mammals hall.

places.name: American Museum of Natural History, New York
places.note: A mounted skeleton among the Ice Age mammals.

sightings.tip: Compare the canines with the lower jaw: it could open its mouth to about 120 degrees, nearly twice as wide as a lion.

summary.text: Smilodon is a genus of extinct felids. It is one of the best-known saber-toothed predators and prehistoric mammals. Although commonly known as the saber-toothed tiger, it was not closely related to the tiger or other modern cats, belonging to the extinct subfamily Machairodontinae, with an estimated date of divergence from the ancestor of living cats around 20 million years ago. Smilodon was one of the last surviving machairodonts alongside Homotherium. Smilodon lived in the Americas during the Pleistocene to early Holocene epoch. The genus was named in 1842 based on fossils from Brazil; the generic name means 'scalpel' or 'two-edged knife' combined with 'tooth'. Three species are recognized today: S. gracilis, S. fatalis, and S. populator. The two latter species were probably descended from S. gracilis, which itself probably evolved from Megantereon. The hundreds of specimens obtained from the La Brea Tar Pits in Los Angeles constitute the largest collection of Smilodon fossils.
